title: Covert administration and altering medicines
blurb: Know when hiding a medicine in food or drink is lawful, who must agree, and why crushing needs a pharmacist first.
question: Winifred, 84, has advanced dementia and lives in a care home. She has started spitting out her anticonvulsant and pushing the cup away. A care assistant suggests crushing it into her yoghurt so she will not notice. What must happen before any medicine is given covertly?

teach.body: Formally, covert administration is the defined process in which a formal decision has been made between healthcare professionals and carers for medicines to be given in a disguised format, without the knowledge or consent of a person who lacks mental capacity. In plain English: hiding a medicine in food, drink or a feeding tube so the person does not know they are taking it, after a proper, recorded team decision.
teach.cite: RPS/RCN Administration of medicines (2019) glossary; CQC covert administration page (2022)

teach.body: A person who has capacity to decide about a medicine has the right to refuse it, even if the refusal looks ill-judged to staff or family. Covert administration must not be used for anyone with capacity. RPS/RCN guidance says medicines are given covertly to people who actively refuse their medication and are considered to lack capacity, in accordance with an agreed management plan. Capacity is assessed under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 for this specific decision at this time.
teach.cite: RPS/RCN 2019 paras 21–23; NICE SC1 rec 1.15.1; MCA 2005 ss1–3

teach.h: Is covert administration even on the table?

root.label: Person refuses a medicine
root.sub: First explore why: taste, swallowing, side effects, fear

teach.caption: CQC: covert administration must be the least restrictive option after trying all others, such as a different formulation or time of day.

teach.caption: NICE SC1 1.15.3 sets out capacity assessment, a best interests meeting including a pharmacist, a recorded plan and regular review for care homes; CQC adds medicine-by-medicine pharmaceutical advice and MAR records. The RPS/RCN guidance applies the same principles in every healthcare setting.

teach.h: Who is in the best interests decision?
head: Person
Why they are there
rows: Know the person and the refusals
Decides if each medicine is still needed
Advises on crushing, mixing and timing
Brings the person's wishes and values
teach.caption: CQC: the decision must be multidisciplinary and must not be taken alone. The meeting can be held remotely if who attended and what was agreed are recorded.

teach.h: Why crushing is a pharmaceutical decision
teach.body: Crushing a tablet or opening a capsule may make its use off-licence, and the prescriber must be told. It can change how the body handles the drug. CQC gives the example of a tablet designed to release slowly over 24 hours: crushed, the whole dose is released at once, risking overdose or more side effects. Some medicines also become ineffective when mixed with certain foods or drinks. So take pharmacist advice for every medicine before altering it, whether or not it is being given covertly.
teach.cite: CQC covert administration (updated 3 November 2022); RPS 2011 crushing guidance cited in RPS/RCN 2019

teach.h: Covert versus simply altering a medicine

rows.label: Licence
values: May be off-licence if crushed or opened

teach.h: Scenario: Winifred in the care home
teach.body: Winifred refuses her anticonvulsant. Her named nurse, Kofi, first tries a different time, a liquid and a familiar carer. Refusals continue. The GP assesses that Winifred cannot understand or weigh the consequences of refusing, and records this. Kofi arranges a best interests meeting with the GP, the community pharmacist and Winifred's son. They agree the medicine is essential; the pharmacist confirms the liquid can be mixed with a small amount of yoghurt. The plan is written into her care plan, the MAR shows covert doses, and a review date is set.

teach.h: Keeping it lawful after the decision
items: Decide medicine by medicine: a new medicine or dose change means a fresh best interests decision.
Use covert administration for as short a time as possible and set review dates based on the person's circumstances.
If capacity fluctuates, use the covert plan at times the person lacks capacity, and record which doses were covert.
Consider whether covert medicines, such as sedatives, add to a deprivation of liberty.
Follow organisational policy: RPS/RCN expects policies and procedures covering covert administration.

teach.text: Do not mix up the two problems. A person WITH capacity who refuses: respect the refusal and tell the prescriber. A person WITHOUT capacity who refuses: covert administration may be considered, but only after a best interests decision and pharmacist advice, never by one nurse's choice at the bedside.

items: Covert means disguised without the person's knowledge; it is for people who lack capacity and actively refuse.
Never covertly medicate a person who has capacity; their refusal stands.
Steps: capacity assessment, best interests meeting (staff, prescriber, pharmacist, family or advocate), written plan, MAR records, regular review.
Crushing or opening may make use off-licence: get pharmacist advice and tell the prescriber.
Each new medicine or dose change needs its own best interests decision.

summary: You can now decide when covert administration is lawful, name who must be involved in the best interests decision and what the plan must contain. You can also explain why crushing or opening a medicine needs pharmacist advice and the prescriber's knowledge.

A.q: Mr Okafor, 79, is on a medical ward. He has capacity and refuses his evening statin, saying it gives him muscle aches. His daughter asks the nurse to hide it in his custard. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Arrange a best interests meeting to agree covert administration
Respect his refusal, record it and inform the prescriber
Crush the tablet into his custard as his daughter requests
Ask the daughter to give the tablet so staff are not involved
A.why: A person with capacity has the right to refuse a medicine. Covert administration must not be used if the person has capacity (NICE SC1 1.15.1; RPS/RCN 2019 para 21). Record the refusal and tell the prescriber, who can review the side effect.

whyNot.0: Best interests decisions apply to people who lack capacity; Mr Okafor has capacity, so his own decision stands.
whyNot.2: Disguising a medicine in food for a person with capacity overrides his valid refusal and is not lawful practice.
whyNot.3: Asking a relative to hide it is still covert administration of a refused medicine, and staff remain accountable for knowing it is happening.

A.q: Which professional's advice must be sought about each medicine before it is mixed with food for covert administration?
options: The pharmacist
The care home manager
The safeguarding lead
The speech and language therapist
A.why: NICE SC1 1.15.3 includes a pharmacist in the best interests meeting, and CQC says to take pharmaceutical advice so that medicines remain safe and effective when given covertly.

whyNot.1: The manager oversees policy but cannot advise whether a formulation can be crushed or mixed safely.
whyNot.2: The safeguarding lead may be involved if there are concerns about restriction, but cannot give pharmaceutical advice on formulations.
whyNot.3: A speech and language therapist assesses swallowing; whether a medicine stays effective when crushed or mixed is a pharmaceutical question.

A.q: A nurse is about to crush a prolonged-release tablet for a patient with swallowing difficulty. What is the main clinical risk of doing this?
options: The tablet will lose its effect within the hour
The whole dose may be released at once, causing toxicity
The patient is likely to develop an allergy to the crushed form
Crushed tablets cannot be absorbed from the stomach
A.why: CQC gives this exact example: crushing a tablet designed to release slowly over 24 hours may release the whole dose too quickly, risking overdose or increased adverse effects. Pharmacist advice is needed first.

whyNot.0: Losing effect is a risk with some medicines mixed with certain foods, but the main danger with a crushed prolonged-release tablet is dose dumping.
whyNot.2: Crushing does not create a new allergy; the risk is the speed at which the drug is released.
whyNot.3: Crushed medicines are often absorbed faster, not blocked, which is why a slow-release product becomes dangerous.

B.q: Grace, 88, lives in a care home and lacks capacity to decide about her medicines. A best interests meeting agreed covert administration of her antipsychotic last month. The GP has now added an antibiotic for a chest infection. What should happen before the antibiotic is given covertly?
options: Give it covertly under the existing plan for the antipsychotic
Ask Grace's son to sign consent for the antibiotic on her behalf
Make a new, recorded best interests decision
Wait until her next scheduled review of the covert plan
B.why: CQC: the need for covert administration must be identified for each medicine; each time a medicine is added or a dose changes, identify the need again and make and record a further best interests decision. Pharmacist advice is needed for the new medicine too.

whyNot.0: The existing plan covers the antipsychotic; the decision is medicine-specific, so it does not extend to a new antibiotic.
whyNot.1: A relative cannot consent for an adult unless they hold a relevant registered LPA; the lawful route here is a best interests decision.
whyNot.3: A chest infection needs timely treatment; the new medicine needs its own decision now, not at the next routine review.

B.q: Under NICE SC1, which element must be included in the process for covert administration in a care home?
options: A Court of Protection order before the first covert dose
Written consent from the person's nearest relative
A second nurse to witness every covert dose given
A record of why incapacity is presumed, and the plan
B.why: NICE SC1 1.15.3 lists: assess capacity, hold a best interests meeting, record the reasons for presuming incapacity and the proposed management plan, plan how medicines will be given, and review regularly.

whyNot.0: A court order is not a routine requirement; the MCA best interests process is the framework.
whyNot.1: Relatives are consulted in the best interests meeting, but their written consent does not authorise treatment of an adult.
whyNot.2: A second witness is a controlled drug requirement in many settings, not a standard element of the covert process in SC1.

B.q: Joseph, 76, has vascular dementia with fluctuating capacity. A covert plan exists for his anticoagulant. This morning he understands what the tablet is for and refuses it. What should the nurse do?
options: Give it covertly in his porridge, as his written plan states
Delay the dose by two hours and then give it covertly as planned
Ask a colleague to keep persuading him until he agrees
Respect today's refusal, record it and inform the prescriber
B.why: CQC: where capacity fluctuates, the covert plan must be used only when the person lacks capacity. When Joseph has capacity his refusal stands; the nurse records it and tells the prescriber because a missed anticoagulant matters clinically.

whyNot.0: The plan applies at times he lacks capacity; using it while he has capacity overrides a valid refusal.
whyNot.1: Waiting and then hiding the dose still overrides a capacitous refusal unless capacity has genuinely been lost and reassessed.
whyNot.2: Repeated pressure to accept undermines a voluntary decision; information and support are fine, persuasion until he gives in is not.

C.q: Ruth, 91, has advanced Alzheimer's disease and lives in a nursing home. She spits out her levothyroxine. The nurse finds she dislikes the taste, and a liquid form is refused too. The GP assesses that she lacks capacity for this decision. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Begin covert administration in tea and document it on the MAR chart
Stop the levothyroxine because Ruth's refusals are persistent
Hold a best interests meeting with GP, pharmacist and family
Refer Ruth for a deprivation of liberty authorisation first
C.why: Capacity has been assessed and alternatives tried. The next step is a multidisciplinary best interests meeting (care staff, prescriber, pharmacist, family or advocate) to decide whether covert administration is in her best interests (NICE SC1 1.15.3; CQC).

whyNot.0: Starting covert doses before a best interests decision and pharmacist advice skips the safeguards; the decision must not be taken alone.
whyNot.1: Stopping an essential medicine is a prescriber's decision and may not be in her best interests; the team should decide together.
whyNot.3: Deprivation of liberty should be considered as part of the plan, but it is not the step that authorises covert medication.

C.q: A best interests meeting agrees covert administration for Malik, 70, who has a severe brain injury. Which entry is most important in his medicines administration record?
options: Which medicines were given covertly and when
The name of the family member who agreed
The brand and amount of food used on each occasion
A note that the nurse had no concerns
C.why: CQC: medicines administration records should clearly record which medicines are administered covertly and when, which matters especially when capacity fluctuates.

whyNot.1: Who attended the meeting belongs in the best interests record, not on every MAR entry.
whyNot.2: The care plan describes how the medicine is given; the brand of food each time is not the key record.
whyNot.3: A general reassurance note does not show which doses were disguised, which is what the record must show.

C.q: Ellen, 82, has capacity and difficulty swallowing tablets after a stroke. She asks the nurse to crush her tablets into jam. She is happy to take them this way. What should the nurse do first?
options: Crush the tablets because Ellen has given her consent
Start a covert administration plan to record the crushing
Ask the speech and language therapist to approve the jam
Get pharmacist advice and tell the prescriber first
C.why: Ellen knows and agrees, so this is not covert. But altering a medicine may make its use off-licence and change its effect, so pharmacist advice is needed and the prescriber must be told (CQC; RPS 2011 crushing guidance).

whyNot.0: Consent covers her wish to take them this way, but it does not show each tablet is safe to crush; that needs pharmacist advice.
whyNot.1: Covert administration is for people who lack capacity and do not know; Ellen is fully aware and agrees.
whyNot.2: SALT input on swallowing is helpful, but whether the medicines can be crushed safely is a pharmaceutical question.

reteach.title: Three gates before a hidden dose
reteach.question: Think of covert administration as a corridor with three locked gates. Which keys open each one?

blocks.body: Gate 1, capacity: has the person been assessed as lacking capacity for this medicine decision? If they have capacity, the corridor ends: respect the refusal. Gate 2, best interests: has a team (staff, prescriber, pharmacist, family or advocate) agreed that this essential medicine should be given covertly? Gate 3, pharmacy: has a pharmacist confirmed how this medicine can be safely given in food or drink?

blocks.text: A relative's agreement is not one of the keys. Families are consulted in the best interests meeting, but they cannot consent for an adult unless they hold a relevant registered LPA.

explain.h: Capacity and the right to refuse
explain.body: When a person has capacity to decide about a medicine they may refuse it, even unwisely. Covert administration is only considered for people who actively refuse and lack capacity, assessed under the MCA 2005 for that decision.

test.q: Which person could be considered for covert administration?
options: A man with capacity who refuses insulin because he dislikes injections
A woman with dementia who lacks capacity and refuses vital medicine
A teenager with capacity who forgets her inhaler at school
A man with depression who has capacity and refuses an antidepressant
test.why: Covert administration is for people who actively refuse medication and lack capacity (RPS/RCN 2019 para 21), where the medicine is essential (CQC).

whyNot.0: He has capacity, so his refusal must be respected.
whyNot.2: Forgetting is not refusal and she has capacity; support and reminders are needed.
whyNot.3: A diagnosis of depression does not remove capacity; with capacity his refusal stands.

explain.body: A multidisciplinary decision: care staff, the prescriber, a pharmacist and a family member or advocate. It can be held remotely if attendance and decisions are recorded. It must not be one person's decision.

test.q: A care home nurse lists people for a covert administration best interests meeting. Who is a required participant under NICE SC1?
options: A pharmacist
The local coroner
A police officer
The CQC inspector
test.why: NICE SC1 1.15.3: care home staff, the prescriber, a pharmacist and a family member or advocate.

whyNot.1: The coroner investigates certain deaths and has no role in medicines decisions for the living.
whyNot.2: Police have no role in a best interests decision about medicines.
whyNot.3: CQC regulates the service and inspects records but does not take part in individual decisions.

explain.body: Crushing tablets or opening capsules may make use off-licence; tell the prescriber and get pharmacist advice. Slow-release products can dump the whole dose when crushed, and some medicines lose effect in certain foods.

test.q: Why must the prescriber be told when a tablet is crushed before administration?
options: Crushing may make the use off-licence
Crushed tablets must be re-dispensed by pharmacy
Crushing changes the medicine's legal category
The prescription must be rewritten as a liquid
test.why: CQC: crushing a tablet or opening a capsule may make its use off-licence, and you must tell the prescriber.

whyNot.1: Pharmacy advice is needed, but crushing does not require the medicine to be re-dispensed.
whyNot.2: The legal category (POM, P, GSL, CD) is unchanged by crushing.
whyNot.3: A liquid may be a better option, but crushing itself does not legally require a new liquid prescription.

explain.body: Write a medicine care plan (how it is given, in what, specialist advice). MAR records show which medicines were given covertly and when. Use covert administration for as short a time as possible and review formally, with review dates set by the person's circumstances.

items: Covert doses recorded on the MAR
Regular formal review of need and capacity

test.q: Six months after covert administration began, a nurse reviews the plan for Hamid, 80. What is the main purpose of this review?
options: To confirm whether covert administration is still needed
To renew the family's consent for another six months
To switch every medicine to a liquid formulation
To transfer responsibility for the plan to the pharmacist
test.why: CQC: schedule regular formal reviews to confirm whether covert administration is still needed, and review capacity assessments.

whyNot.1: Family views inform best interests, but the family does not give consent that needs renewing.
whyNot.2: Formulation changes are made medicine by medicine on pharmacist advice, not as the purpose of review.
whyNot.3: The plan remains a multidisciplinary responsibility; the pharmacist advises but does not take it over.
